newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatian rail workers restart passenger traffic.
newsitem.headline: Croatian rail workers restart passenger traffic.

text.p: Croatian railway workers, on strike for the sixth day running, restarted passenger services on Wednesday "as a token of good will" after a colleague, who had been sacked, was allowed to return to work.

"All passenger trains moved at 1300 (1100 gmt)," said a dispatcher at the main Zagreb railway station. But freight trains, except for those carrying supplies for the Croatian army and NATO peacekeepers in neighbouring Bosnia, remained on halt.

One of the leaders of the railway workers trade union, Josip Puskaric, said the striking committee decided to start moving passenger trains after one railman -- sacked by the railway company on Monday -- was allowed to return to his job.
"It is a token of our good will towards the government and the passengers," Puskaric told Reuters. "We are not giving up our demands."

Eighty percent of Croatian rail traffic was halted on November 28 when 11,000 employees of the state-run Hrvatske Zeljeznice (HZ) began a national strike for wage increases and better working conditions.
They maintained only a legally required minimum of trains, but on Tuesday the strike was extended in defiance of pressure by the HZ for a return to work.
Strikers decided to suspend all non-military traffic after HZ sacked a railman who refused to return to work on Monday, which they saw as an infringment of their legal rights.
The railway company has denied threatening to sack workers who refused to sign written statements criticising the strike.
HZ said it was losing an estimated 1.6 million kuna (about $300,000) a day due to the stoppage and risked being unable to pay wages for November.
Loss-making HZ receives more than a billion kuna ($200 million) from the 1996 budget and the government said it would try to keep the subsidy under one-billion kuna level in 1997.
The government, faced with a wave of unrest, refused to give in to the strikers' demands and said there was no money to increase pay this year.
But at its session on Wednesday the government urged a comission appointed by the transport Ministry to "negotiate with all unions in order to regularise traffic".
Puskaric said he was optimistic talks with the government would start soon. "We expect reason to prevail," he said.
